changes.before: You cannot show you got better with no start.
changes.after: Keeping a starting piece helps you show what changed.

changes.before: Read the four-word rule once and leave it on the board. Three for what works, one for not yet. Pupils who miss the fourth word have no baseline to improve against.
changes.after: Model three strengths and one next step. These words support the comparison; a missing word does not erase the starting work. Accept speech, pointing or a recorded response.

changes.before: Two pieces, and one of them is a baseline
changes.after: Two pieces, and one is easier to compare

changes.before: Only one of them can be used.
changes.after: Both show a start. Notes help you explain the change.

changes.before: The piece with words shows what changed.
changes.after: The piece with words records what the maker noticed.

changes.before: Each card holds one word from a real baseline.
changes.after: Each card holds a word from a teaching example.

changes.before: Rubbish is about the maker, not the work.
changes.after: Rubbish is a judgement with no detail to act on.

changes.before: ABOUT THE MAKER
changes.after: NEEDS MORE DETAIL

changes.before: Success evidence: one skill card with one skill named, one measure with a number in it, the proof page named, and today's date.
changes.after: Success evidence: one chosen skill, a checkable goal, the proof page and today's date on your card.

changes.before: A skill is one thing your hands do
changes.after: A skill is one action you can practise

changes.before: A skill is one thing your hands do.
changes.after: A skill is one action you can practise.

changes.before: Shading is a skill. Art is not a skill.
changes.after: Shading is a skill. Art is too broad for this small goal.

changes.before: Art is a whole art form, and it is too big.
changes.after: Name one action in your chosen art form.

changes.before: How means the measure still needs a number.
changes.after: How means the measure needs a clear check.

changes.before: Then help them add one number, and only one.
changes.after: Help them name a count or a feature to look for.

changes.before: Two skills on one card is two cards, and both get dropped.
changes.after: If two skills appear, choose one to focus on first.

changes.before: 2 · put a number in the measure.
changes.after: 2 · name a count or a visible feature to check.

changes.before: Write your measure under it, with a number in it.
changes.after: Write your measure: a count or a feature to check.

changes.before: Extend · name one skill, write a measure with a number in it, and name the proof page.
changes.after: Extend · name one skill, write a checkable measure, and name the proof page.

changes.before: A card with no date cannot be checked later.
changes.after: Add a date so the stages of your work are easy to follow.

changes.before: If you cannot, add a number and say it again.
changes.after: If the check is unclear, name what they should look for.

changes.before: One skill is named, and it is one thing the hands do rather than a whole art form.
changes.after: One specific arts skill is named, with a clear action to practise.

changes.before: The measure carries a number or a can-do, so somebody else could count it.
changes.after: The measure names a count or a feature that someone else can check.

changes.before: Name one skill, write a measure with a number in it, and name the proof page.
changes.after: Name one skill, write a checkable measure, and name the proof page.

changes.before: One attempt shows nothing
changes.after: One attempt records a start

changes.before: One attempt on its own shows nothing.
changes.after: One attempt records a starting point.

changes.before: A record you cannot read is not evidence.
changes.after: Make the order clear so someone else can follow your practice.

changes.before: Model the stop, not the drawing. Pupils copy the timing. If you let box one run long, every strip in the room becomes uncomparable and the whole record is lost.
changes.after: Model the tool action and the stop. Similar trial times help comparison. If a trial runs longer, note that change and discuss what it may explain; keep the genuine record.

changes.before: Same skill, and only one strip proves anything
changes.after: Like-sized trials make the change easier to explain

changes.before: Then the only thing left changing is you.
changes.after: This makes it easier to judge what practice changed.

changes.before: It is not praise. Specific praise can show what to keep. A clear next step shows what to try.
changes.after: Specific praise can show what to keep. A clear next step shows what to try.

changes.before: Say the one-piece rule out loud and leave it on the board. Choosing one next step helps pupils use feedback without having to act on every comment at once, and the record then shows a heap of talk rather than a change.
changes.after: Model one next step. Pupils may hear several comments and choose one useful action. Keep the speaker’s words and the pupil’s choice clear.

changes.before: Then I ask him one sharp question about it.
changes.after: Then I ask my partner one clear question about it.

changes.before: One change can be proved. Ten changes cannot.
changes.after: One planned change is easier to explain than several at once.

changes.before: With no before, what it did cannot be shown.
changes.after: A kept before state helps us show what this change did.

changes.before: photo or ring made first
changes.after: photo, copy or unchanged sample

changes.before: Find the adult who gave you the feedback line.
changes.after: Find the person who gave you the feedback line.

changes.before: That is your proof that the line was used.
changes.after: Keep their response beside your before and after record.

changes.before: It is not a fail, and I write it down.
changes.after: This describes my practice goal, not my award result.

changes.before: Proof that cannot be found does not count.
changes.after: Add a clear locator so the adviser can find and check it.

changes.before: A locator is not extra work. It is the proof.
changes.after: A locator points to the work that gives the proof.

changes.before: Your words told them where to look.
changes.after: Your words help them find the work. Choose one next step together: clarify the locator or name your next skill.

changes.before: The job is to notice, and to write it down.
changes.after: Notice a choice and record it by speech, sketch or writing.

changes.before: That is a choice about scale.
changes.after: That is a choice about line, tone and composition.

changes.before: Later is too late. Later turns into it was good.
changes.after: A quick note can help you recall the detail later.

changes.before: Those words tell a reader nothing about the work.
changes.after: These views need a detail from the work to explain them.

changes.before: You may not use nice, weird or boring.
changes.after: You may give your honest view. Add a detail to explain it.

changes.before: Use all four labels if you can.
changes.after: Use the labels that fit the work. Do not invent a sound or material you cannot check.

changes.before: If any choice would give the same effect, the row is weak.
changes.after: If you cannot point to the choice that led to your view, the link needs more detail.

changes.before: So change the effect until it follows the choice.
changes.after: Look at the work again. Keep your own response and make the link clear. If the work does not support that link, change the claim or choose another example.

changes.before: It was lovely fails it. Thick black ink did not make it lovely.
changes.after: It was lovely needs a detail and a reason. Say which choice led to that view for you.

changes.before: Before the lesson, prepare a named, checked source pack with at least two genuine choices. Suggested public primary sources: Barbara Hepworth Estate, Biography, https://barbarahepworth.org.uk/biography/ (1903, 1921–24 and 1925 entries); its home page and linked Assembly of Sea Forms record, https://barbarahepworth.org.uk/; Henry Moore Foundation, Discover Henry Moore, https://henry-moore.org/discover-and-research/discover-henry-moore/, and Henry Moore’s story, https://henry-moore.org/discover-and-research/discover-henry-moore/henry-moores-story/. These are research sources, not places to visit. Staff check each selected passage, work caption and public URL before use. Give each artist a page with a clearly credited work image or accessible description, its title and medium, and short, faithful source extracts covering practice, career, life and work. Keep the original beside any plain-language gloss. Number the pack pages and identify the publisher, page title, URL and section on each. Select art-relevant public life facts, such as where an artist worked; omit distressing biographical detail. Have large print and a read-aloud version ready. No invented fallback artist or biography: if a source fails, use a second checked source. The model below is conditional on the checked Hepworth pages being in hand; otherwise model the same process with the actual pack and its exact facts. The deck does not certify a local pack as prepared.

changes.before: Keep your source note and next question together. Next time, you will build a fuller picture of this real person’s practice, career, life and work.
changes.after: Tell your checking partner which question you want to research next. Keep it beside your source note. Next time, you will find more about this real person’s practice, career, life and work.

changes.before: One measure with a number in it, starting with the words I can
changes.after: One checkable measure, starting with the words I can

changes.before: Boxes labelled ABOUT THE WORK, ABOUT THE MAKER. Same piece, and only one kind of word can be checked
changes.after: Two feedback notes: one points to a visible detail; one judgement needs more detail.

changes.before: Boxes labelled ONE THING CHANGES, THREE THINGS CHANGE. Same skill, and only one strip proves anything
changes.after: Two practice records: a comparable pair makes it easier to judge what changed.

changes.before: the change left is your practice
changes.after: easier to judge what practice changed

changes.before: Give a ring-and-date option to any pupil with no photo. They ring the part on the log page first and write the week number in the ring.
changes.after: If a photo is not available, keep a copy or unchanged sample. Leave the original as it is and try the change on a fresh test piece. A ring locates a part; it does not preserve marks that are changed.
